Learning Objectives

How do programming languages deal with concurrent execution?

- Describe threads and shared mutable state
- Identify race conditions and data races
- Apply synchronization mechanisms: locks, synchronized blocks, and atomic operations
- Describe higher-level concurrency abstractions in Java
- Compare concurrency approaches across languages

- Modern hardware has multiple cores — sequential programs waste resources
- Many problems are naturally concurrent: web servers, GUIs, simulations

Concurrency vs. parallelism:
○ Concurrency: dealing with multiple things at once (structure)
○ Parallelism: doing multiple things at once (execution)

Java Threads: The Basics

A thread is a lightweight unit of execution.

```java
public class HelloThread {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Thread t = new Thread(() -> {
            System.out.println("Hello from thread: "
                    + Thread.currentThread().getName());
        });
        t.start();
        System.out.println("Hello from main: "
                + Thread.currentThread().getName());
    }
}
```

$ javac HelloThread.java && java HelloThread
Hello from main: main
Hello from thread: Thread-0

============================================================
时间戳: 00:10:17 (617.00s)

Java Threads: The Basics

A thread is a lightweight unit of execution.

```java
public class HelloThread {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Thread t = new Thread(() -> {
            System.out.println("Hello from thread: "
                    + Thread.currentThread().getName());
        });
        t.start();
        System.out.println("Hello from main: "
                + Thread.currentThread().getName());
    }
}
```

$ javac HelloThread.java && java HelloThread
Hello from main: main
Hello from thread: Thread-0

Shared Mutable State

What happens when two threads modify the same variable?

```java
public class Counter {
    static int count = 0;

    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        Thread t1 = new Thread(() -> {
            for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) count++;
        });
        Thread t2 = new Thread(() -> {
            for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) count++;
        });
        t1.start(); t2.start();
        t1.join();  t2.join();
        System.out.println("count = " + count);
    }
}
```

$ java Counter
count = 137462 # Expected 200000!

============================================================
时间戳: 00:12:07 (727.00s)
============================================================

    static int count = 0;

    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        Thread t1 = new Thread(() -> {
            for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) count++;
        });
        Thread t2 = new Thread(() -> {
            for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) count++;
        });
        t1.start(); t2.start();
        t1.join();  t2.join();
        System.out.println("count = " + count);
    }
}
```

$ java Counter
count = 137462 # Expected 200000!

What happens when two threads modify the same variable?

```java
public class Counter {
    static int count = 0;

    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        Thread t1 = new Thread(() -> {
            for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) count++;
        });
        Thread t2 = new Thread(() -> {
            for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) count++;
        });
        t1.start(); t2.start();
        t1.join();  t2.join();
        System.out.println("count = " + count);
    }
}
```

$ java Counter
count = 137462 # Expected 200000!

Race condition! The result is different every time.
5

============================================================
时间戳: 00:14:32 (872.00s)

Shared Mutable State

What happens when two threads modify the same variable?

```java
public class Counter {
    static int count = 0;

    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        Thread t1 = new Thread(() -> {
            for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) count++;
        });
        Thread t2 = new Thread(() -> {
            for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) count++;
        });
        t1.start(); t2.start();
        t1.join();  t2.join();
        System.out.println("count = " + count);
    }
}
```

时间戳: 00:17:58 (1078.00s)
============================================================
Synchronization: Locks

A lock (mutex) ensures only one thread accesses a critical section at a time.

```java
public class SyncCounter {
    static int count = 0;
    static final Object lock = new Object();

    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        Thread t1 = new Thread(() -> {
            for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++)
                synchronized (lock) { count++; }
        });
        Thread t2 = new Thread(() -> {
            for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++)
                synchronized (lock) { count++; }
        });
        t1.start(); t2.start();
        t1.join();  t2.join();
        System.out.println("count = " + count);
    }
}
```

$ java SyncCounter
count = 200000     # Correct every time!

A lock (mutex) ensures only one thread accesses a critical section at a time.

```java
public class SyncCounter {
    static int count = 0;
    static final Object lock = new Object();

    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        Thread t1 = new Thread(() -> {
            for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++)
                synchronized (lock) { count++; }
        });
        Thread t2 = new Thread(() -> {
            for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++)
                synchronized (lock) { count++; }
        });
        t1.start(); t2.start();
        t1.join();  t2.join();
        System.out.println("count = " + count);
    }
}
```

$ java SyncCounter
count = 200000     # Correct every time!
```

A lock (mutex) ensures only one thread accesses a critical section at a time.

```java
public class SyncCounter {
    static int count = 0;
    static final Object lock = new Object();

    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        Thread t1 = new Thread(() -> {
            for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++)
                synchronized (lock) { count++; }
        });
        Thread t2 = new Thread(() -> {
            for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++)
                synchronized (lock) { count++; }
        });
        t1.start(); t2.start();
        t1.join();  t2.join();
        System.out.println("count = " + count);
    }
}
```

$ java SyncCounter
count = 200000     # Correct every time!
```

============================================================
synchronized Methods

Java also lets you synchronize entire methods.

```java
public class BankAccount {
    private int balance;

    public BankAccount(int initial) { this.balance = initial; }

    public synchronized void deposit(int amount) {
        balance += amount;
    }

    public synchronized void withdraw(int amount) {
        if (balance >= amount) {
            balance -= amount;
        }
    }

    public synchronized int getBalance() {
        return balance;
    }
}
```

synchronized on a method locks on this — only one thread can execute any synchronized method on that object at a time.

        balance += amount;
    }

    public synchronized void withdraw(int amount) {
        if (balance >= amount) {
            balance -= amount;
        }
    }

    public synchronized int getBalance() {
        return balance;
    }
}
```

synchronized on a method locks on this — only one thread can execute any synchronized method on that object at a time.

============================================================
Deadlock

What happens when two threads each wait for the other's lock?

```java
public class Deadlock {
    static final Object lockA = new Object();
    static final Object lockB = new Object();

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Thread t1 = new Thread(() -> {
            synchronized (lockA) {
                synchronized (lockB) { System.out.println("t1"); }
            }
        });
        Thread t2 = new Thread(() -> {
            synchronized (lockB) {
                synchronized (lockA) { System.out.println("t2"); }
            }
        });
        t1.start(); t2.start();
    }
}
```

Functional programming avoids the problem: immutable data can be freely shared.

Atomic Operations

For simple operations, Java provides lock-free atomic classes.

```java
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

public class AtomicCounter {
    static AtomicInteger count = new AtomicInteger(0);

    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        Thread t1 = new Thread(() -> {
            for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) count.incrementAndGet();
        });
        Thread t2 = new Thread(() -> {
            for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) count.incrementAndGet();
        });
        t1.start(); t2.start();
        t1.join(); t2.join();
        System.out.println("count = " + count.get());
    }
}
```

$ java AtomicCounter
count = 200000

Atomic Operations

For simple operations, Java provides lock-free atomic classes.

```java
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

public class AtomicCounter {
    static AtomicInteger count = new AtomicInteger(0);

    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        Thread t1 = new Thread(() -> {
            for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) count.incrementAndGet();
        });
        Thread t2 = new Thread(() -> {
            for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) count.incrementAndGet();
        });
        t1.start(); t2.start();
        t1.join(); t2.join();
        System.out.println("count = " + count.get());
    }
}
```

$ java AtomicCounter
count = 200000

volatile Keyword

What about visibility between threads?

```java
public class Visibility {
    static boolean running = true;   // not volatile!

    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        Thread t = new Thread(() -> {
            while (running) { /* spin */ }
            System.out.println("Stopped!");
        });
        t.start();
        Thread.sleep(100);
        running = false;   // might never be seen by t!
    }
}
```

Without `volatile`, the JVM may cache `running` in a register — the thread never sees the update!

The Java Memory Model

Why do we need a memory model?
- Modern CPUs reorder instructions and cache memory for performance
- Without rules, threads might see stale or inconsistent data
- The Java Memory Model (JMM) defines happens-before relationships:
  - Unlock on a monitor happens-before subsequent lock on that monitor
  - Write to volatile field happens-before subsequent read
  - Thread.start() happens-before any action in the started thread
  - All actions in a thread happen-before Thread.join() returns

  - Thread.start() happens-before any action in the started thread
  - All actions in a thread happen-before Thread.join() returns

时间戳: 00:29:02 (1742.00s)
============================================================
Thread Pools: Don't Create Raw Threads

💡 Creating a thread per task is wasteful. Use a thread pool.

```java
import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class PoolExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4);

        List<Future<Integer>> futures = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
            final int n = i;
            futures.add(pool.submit(() -> {
                Thread.sleep(100);
                return n * n;
            }));
        }
        for (Future<Integer> f : futures) {
            System.out.println(f.get());   // blocks until result ready
        }
        pool.shutdown();
    }
}
```

时间戳: 00:29:08 (1748.00s)
============================================================
Thread Pools: Don't Create Raw Threads

💡 Creating a thread per task is wasteful. Use a thread pool.

```java
import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class PoolExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4);

        List<Future<Integer>> futures = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
            final int n = i;
            futures.add(pool.submit(() -> {
                Thread.sleep(100);
                return n * n;
            }));
        }
        for (Future<Integer> f : futures) {
            System.out.println(f.get());   // blocks until result ready
        }
        pool.shutdown();
    }
}
```

💡 Creating a thread per task is wasteful. Use a thread pool.

```java
import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class PoolExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4);

        List<Future<Integer>> futures = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
            final int n = i;
            futures.add(pool.submit(() -> {
                Thread.sleep(100);
                return n * n;
            }));
        }
        for (Future<Integer> f : futures) {
            System.out.println(f.get());   // blocks until result ready
        }
        pool.shutdown();
    }
}
```

                Thread.sleep(100);
                return n * n;
            }));
        }
        for (Future<Integer> f : futures) {
            System.out.println(f.get());   // blocks until result ready
        }
        pool.shutdown();
    }
}
```

ExecutorService manages a pool of reusable threads.

Thread Pools: Don't Create Raw Threads

Creating a thread per task is wasteful. Use a thread pool.

```java
import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class PoolExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4);

        List<Future<Integer>> futures = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
            final int n = i;
            futures.add(pool.submit(() -> {
                Thread.sleep(100);
                return n * n;
            }));
        }
        for (Future<Integer> f : futures) {
            System.out.println(f.get());   // blocks until result ready
        }
        pool.shutdown();
    }
}
```

**CompletableFuture: Composable Async**

CompletableFuture lets you chain async operations — functional style!

```java
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;

public class AsyncChain {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        CompletableFuture
            .supplyAsync(() -> "Hello")
            .thenApply(s -> s + " World")
            .thenApply(String::toUpperCase)
            .thenAccept(System.out::println)
            .join();  // wait for completion
    }
}
```

**CompletableFuture: Composable Async**

CompletableFuture lets you chain async operations — functional style!

```java
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;

public class AsyncChain {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        CompletableFuture
            .supplyAsync(() -> "Hello")
            .thenApply(s -> s + " World")
            .thenApply(String::toUpperCase)
            .thenAccept(System.out::println)
            .join();  // wait for completion
    }
}
```

4 // Two threads modifying:
5 // → ConcurrentModificationException

6 // → correct behavior, no locks needed

4 // Two threads modifying:

Safe

2 Map<String, Integer> map =

5 // Two threads modifying:
6 // → correct behavior, no locks needed

Producer-Consumer Pattern

A classic concurrency pattern using BlockingQueue.

```java
import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class ProducerConsumer {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        BlockingQueue<Integer> queue = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(10);

        Thread producer = new Thread(() -> {
            for (int i = 0; i < 20; i++) {
                try {
                    queue.put(i);      // blocks if queue is full
                    System.out.println("Produced: " + i);
                } catch (InterruptedException e) { break; }
            }
        });

        Thread consumer = new Thread(() -> {
            for (int i = 0; i < 20; i++) {
                try {
                    int val = queue.take(); // blocks if queue is empty
                    System.out.println("Consumed: " + val);
                } catch (InterruptedException e) { break; }
            }
        });

        producer.start(); consumer.start();
    }
}
```

时间戳: 00:36:35 (2195.00s)

Collections.synchronizedMap() exists but is coarse-grained — locks the whole map.

============================================================
Producer-Consumer Pattern

A classic concurrency pattern using BlockingQueue.

```java
import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class ProducerConsumer {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        BlockingQueue<Integer> queue = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(10);

        Thread producer = new Thread(() -> {
            for (int i = 0; i < 20; i++) {
                try {
                    queue.put(i);      // blocks if queue is full
                    System.out.println("Produced: " + i);
                } catch (InterruptedException e) { break; }
            }
        });

        Thread consumer = new Thread(() -> {
            for (int i = 0; i < 20; i++) {
                try {
                    int val = queue.take(); // blocks if queue is empty
                    System.out.println("Consumed: " + val);
                } catch (InterruptedException e) { break; }
            }
        });

        producer.start(); consumer.start();
    }
}
```

            for (int i = 0; i < 20; i++) {
                try {
                    int val = queue.take(); // blocks if queue is empty
                    System.out.println("Consumed: " + val);
                } catch (InterruptedException e) { break; }
            }
        });

        producer.start(); consumer.start();
    }
}
```

Producer-Consumer Pattern

A classic concurrency pattern using BlockingQueue.

```java
import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class ProducerConsumer {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        BlockingQueue<Integer> queue = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(10);

        Thread producer = new Thread(() -> {
            for (int i = 0; i < 20; i++) {
                try {
                    queue.put(i);      // blocks if queue is full
                    System.out.println("Produced: " + i);
                } catch (InterruptedException e) { break; }
            }
        });

        Thread consumer = new Thread(() -> {
            for (int i = 0; i < 20; i++) {
                try {
                    int val = queue.take(); // blocks if queue is empty
                    System.out.println("Consumed: " + val);
                } catch (InterruptedException e) { break; }
            }
        });

        producer.start(); consumer.start();
    }
}

Virtual Threads (Java 21+)

Java 21 introduced virtual threads — lightweight, JVM-managed threads.

```java
import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class VirtualThreads {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        try (var executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) {
                final int n = i;
                executor.submit(() -> {
                    Thread.sleep(1000);
                    return n;
                });
            }
            // waits for all tasks to complete
            System.out.println("Done!");
        }
    }
}
```

Virtual Threads (Java 21+)

Java 21 introduced virtual threads — lightweight, JVM-managed threads.

```java
import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class VirtualThreads {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        try (var executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) {
                final int n = i;
                executor.submit(() -> {
                    Thread.sleep(1000);
                    return n;
                });
            }
            // waits for all tasks to complete
            System.out.println("Done!");
        }
    }
}
```

Virtual Threads (Java 21+)

Java 21 introduced virtual threads — lightweight, JVM-managed threads.

```java
import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class VirtualThreads {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        try (var executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) {
                final int n = i;
                executor.submit(() -> {
                    Thread.sleep(1000);
                    return n;
                });
            }
            // waits for all tasks to complete
            System.out.println("Done!");
        }
    }
}
```

Virtual Threads (Java 21+)

Java 21 introduced virtual threads — lightweight, JVM-managed threads.

```java
import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class VirtualThreads {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        try (var executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) {
                final int n = i;
                executor.submit(() -> {
                    Thread.sleep(1000);
                    return n;
                });
            }
            // waits for all tasks to complete
            System.out.println("Done!");
        }
    }
}
```

100,000 OS threads would crash. 100,000 virtual threads is fine!

Virtual threads are extremely cheap and heap-allocated — create one per task, no pooling.

The JVM multiplexes them onto OS threads, unmounting transparently on block. Similar to Go's goroutines.

import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class VirtualThreads {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        try (var executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) {
                final int n = i;
                executor.submit(() -> {
                    Thread.sleep(1000);
                    return n;
                });
            }
            // waits for all tasks to complete
            System.out.println("Done!");
        }
    }
}
```

100,000 OS threads would crash. 100,000 virtual threads is fine!

Virtual threads are extremely cheap and heap-allocated — create one per task, no pooling.

The JVM multiplexes them onto OS threads, unmounting transparently on block. Similar to Go's goroutines.

        try (var executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) {
                final int n = i;
                executor.submit(() -> {
                    Thread.sleep(1000);
                    return n;
                });
            }
            // waits for all tasks to complete
            System.out.println("Done!");
        }
    }
}
```

100,000 OS threads would crash. 100,000 virtual threads is fine!

Virtual threads are extremely cheap and heap-allocated — create one per task, no pooling.

The JVM multiplexes them onto OS threads, unmounting transparently on block. Similar to Go's goroutines.

            for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) {
                final int n = i;
                executor.submit(() -> {
                    Thread.sleep(1000);
                    return n;
                });
            }
            // waits for all tasks to complete
            System.out.println("Done!");
        }
    }
}
```

100,000 OS threads would crash. 100,000 virtual threads is fine!

Virtual threads are extremely cheap and heap-allocated — create one per task, no pooling.

The JVM multiplexes them onto OS threads, unmounting transparently on block. Similar to Go's goroutines.

Concurrency Across Languages

How do other languages approach concurrency?

| Language | Primary Model | Key Idea |
|----------|---------------|----------|
| Java     | Shared memory + locks | Threads share heap; synchronized for safety |
| Scala    | Actors (Akka) / Futures | Message passing; immutable data preferred |
| Rust     | Ownership + Send / Sync | Compiler prevents data races |
| Go       | Goroutines + channels | "Don't communicate by sharing; share by communicating" |
| Erlang   | Actor model | Lightweight processes; no shared state at all |
| JavaScript | Event loop + Promises | Single-threaded; async I/O via callbacks |
| Haskell  | STM (Software Transactional Memory) | Composable atomic transactions |

| Haskell  | STM (Software Transactional Memory) | Composable atomic transactions |

Concurrency Across Languages

How do other languages approach concurrency?

| Haskell  | STM (Software Transactional Memory) | Composable atomic transactions |

Concurrency Across Languages

How do other languages approach concurrency?

| Java     | Shared memory + locks | Threads share heap; synchronized for safety |
| Scala    | Actors (Akka) / Futures | Message passing; immutable data preferred |
| Rust     | Ownership + Send / Sync | Compiler prevents data races |
| Go       | Goroutines + channels | "Don't communicate by sharing; share by communicating" |

| Haskell  | STM (Software Transactional Memory) | Composable atomic transactions |

Concurrency Across Languages

How do other languages approach concurrency?

| Haskell  | STM (Software Transactional Memory) | Composable atomic transactions |

The Functional Perspective

Why does immutability help with concurrency?

Mutable: need synchronization

1 // Shared mutable list - danger!
2 List<String> shared = new ArrayList<>();
3
4 // Thread 1
5 shared.add("hello");
6
7 // Thread 2
8 shared.add("world");
9
10 // -> race condition!

Immutable: freely shareable

1 // Immutable list - no danger!
2 val shared = List("hello", "world")
3
4 // Any thread can read - no locks
5 // No thread can modify - no races

The Functional Perspective

Why does immutability help with concurrency?

Mutable: need synchronization
```
1 // Shared mutable list - danger!
2 List<String> shared = new ArrayList<>();
3
4 // Thread 1
5 shared.add("hello");
6
7 // Thread 2
8 shared.add("world");
9
10 // -> race condition!
```

Immutable: freely shareable
```
1 // Immutable list - no danger!
2 val shared = List("hello", "world")
3
4 // Any thread can read - no locks
5 // No thread can modify - no races
```

Immutable data is inherently thread-safe.
This is why functional programming and concurrency are such natural partners.

2 List<String> shared = new ArrayList<>();
3
4 // Thread 1
5 shared.add("hello");
6
7 // Thread 2
8 shared.add("world");
9
10 // -> race condition!
```

Immutable: freely shareable
```
1 // Immutable list - no danger!
2 val shared = List("hello", "world")
3
4 // Any thread can read - no locks
5 // No thread can modify - no races
```

Immutable data is inherently thread-safe.
This is why functional programming and concurrency are such natural partners.

The Functional Perspective

Why does immutability help with concurrency?

Mutable: need synchronization
```
1 // Shared mutable list - danger!
2 List<String> shared = new ArrayList<>();
3
4 // Thread 1
5 shared.add("hello");
6
7 // Thread 2
8 shared.add("world");
9
10 // -> race condition!
```

Immutable: freely shareable
```
1 // Immutable list - no danger!
2 val shared = List("hello", "world")
3
4 // Any thread can read - no locks
5 // No thread can modify - no races
```

Immutable data is inherently thread-safe.
This is why functional programming and concurrency are such natural partners.

        if (cache == null) {
            cache = new HashMap<>();
            cache.put("greeting", "hello");
        }
        return cache.get(key);
    }
}
```

- Two threads call `get()` at the same time
- Both see `cache == null`
- Both create a new `HashMap`
- One thread's map (and its entries) is lost

Is this fix correct?

```java
public class LazyInit {
    private static volatile Map<String, String> cache;

    public static String get(String key) {
        if (cache == null) {
            synchronized (LazyInit.class) {
                if (cache == null) { // double-checked locking
                    Map<String, String> temp = new HashMap<>();
                    temp.put("greeting", "hello");
                    cache = temp;
                }
            }
        }
        return cache.get(key);
    }
}
```

1. Prefer immutability — immutable objects are always thread-safe
2. Minimize shared mutable state — the less sharing, the fewer bugs
3. Use high-level abstractions — ExecutorService, ConcurrentHashMap, BlockingQueue over raw synchronized
4. Don't reinvent the wheel — java.util.concurrent exists for a reason
5. Make state ownership clear — who is responsible for this data?

============================================================
Summary

- Threads share memory — this is powerful but dangerous.
- Race conditions arise from unsynchronized access to shared mutable state.
- `synchronized` and locks enforce mutual exclusion, but introduce deadlock risks.
- `volatile` ensures visibility between threads, but not atomicity.
- Atomic classes provide lock-free thread-safe operations for simple cases.

- `synchronized` and locks enforce mutual exclusion, but introduce deadlock risks.
- `volatile` ensures visibility between threads, but not atomicity.
- Atomic classes provide lock-free thread-safe operations for simple cases.
- The Java Memory Model defines happens-before rules that govern what threads can see.
- Higher-level abstractions (ExecutorService, CompletableFuture, BlockingQueue) reduce error-prone manual synchronization.
- Virtual threads (Java 21) make thread-per-task practical.
- Immutability is the simplest path to thread safety — functional programming and concurrency are natural partners.
- The concurrency landscape ranges from shared memory (Java/C) to message passing (Go/Erlang) to compile-time enforcement (Rust).

- Atomic classes provide lock-free thread-safe operations for simple cases.
- The Java Memory Model defines happens-before rules that govern what threads can see.
- Higher-level abstractions (ExecutorService, CompletableFuture, BlockingQueue) reduce error-prone manual synchronization.
- Virtual threads (Java 21) make thread-per-task practical.
- Immutability is the simplest path to thread safety — functional programming and concurrency are natural partners.
- The concurrency landscape ranges from shared memory (Java/C) to message passing (Go/Erlang) to compile-time enforcement (Rust).

Page 24 of 24

Question 3 (1 point)
Consider the following JavaScript program.

```javascript
var f;
f = function () {
    console.log ("1");
};
f = function () {
    console.log ("2");
    f ();
};
f ();
```

What is printed to the console when this program is executed? Do not include the value returned (next to the arrow in the browser) in your answer.

1 on the first line and 2 on the second line
2 on the first line and 1 on the second line

The program does not terminate, because the call to f in the second anonymous function refers to whatever the current value of f is in its enclosing scope, i.e., another surprising consequence of using non-final variables from enclosing scope.

Question 4 (1 point)    ✓ Saved
Consider the following JavaScript program.

```javascript
var f;
f = function () {
    console.log ("1");
};
f = (function (h) {
    return function () {
        console.log ("2");
        h ();
    };
});
(f)();
```

What is printed to the console when this program is executed? Do not include the value returned (next to the arrow in the browser) in your answer.

    return function () {
        return function () {
            return function () {
                return function () {
                    console.log("done");
                };
            };
        };
    };
};
```

Which of the following expressions cause "done" to be printed on the console without error?

- f()
- f()()()()

Concepts of Programming Languages (CSC 447)
Spring, AY25/26

This is the course home page for Concepts of Programming Languages for Spring AY25/26.

The course meets on Tuesdays, 5:45pm-9:00pm in person in CDM Room 228.
• Students in Section 901 are expected to attend class in-person.
• Flex students (Section 941) may attend lectures in-person or by joining the Class Zoom Meeting, or watch lectures asynchronously on Course Online.

Grades, quizzes, lecture recordings, homework submission, and announcements can be found at D2L.
Please read the course syllabus.
Please join the course Discord server.
Other resources include CDM Tutors and Student Success at DePaul

Instructor
Eric J. Fredericks
Find me on Discord.
Office Hours: Tuesdays, 4:50pm-5:35pm (Classroom), or Wednesdays, 7:30pm-8:15pm (Zoom)
Office: CDM 228 (Tuesdays), Zoom (Wednesdays)
Zoom: Instructor Zoom Link (for office hours or other pre-arranged meetings)

DEPAUL UNIVERSITY - SCHOOL OF COMPUTING
CSC447 CONCEPTS OF PROGRAMMING LANGUAGES
FINAL EXAM STUDY GUIDE - SPRING AY 2025/2026
Instructor: Eric J. Fredericks
This study guide is intended to help you engage with the course material in preparation for the final exam. While the exercises in this study guide are expressed in the spirit of the final exam, the actual final exam may deviate in any or all questions.
Exercises in this study guide start with a brief summary, a list of resources that may help in answering the question, the actual question, a solution strategy how to approach the question (consult only after attempting an answer), and variations to help you create similar exercises for further practice. In addition, use the Scala REPL and JavaScript Console to work through the exercises.
The exam will have 22 questions (in the spirit of the "Question" paragraphs from the exercises of this guide—no summary, solution strategy, resources, or variations will be listed).
Use the variations in the study guide to challenge your understanding of the material; for example, ask yourself: What code changes would make another answer correct? What happens if the types change? What other almost correct answers might be imagined? How would a different programming language change the answer?
To receive credit:
• Write your name at the top of this page.
• Write your answers on this page. Each answer is a single uppercase letter (A–E); there is precisely one correct answer per question. Write clearly; ambiguous answers will be marked incorrect.
• Upload a PDF of this first page on D2L (accepted format: pdf)

| 6        |        | 19       |        | 32       |

Solution Strategy.
- Determine the free variables of the anonymous function; the closure should have one field per free variable
- Determine variables in the environment to bind these free variables, and note their names (val vs. var)
- val become copied (e.g., int, double, ...), var become references (e.g., scala.runtime.IntRef, scala.runtime.DoubleRef)

2 Serial Number: 10

Exercise 2 Continuation passing is an implementation style that replaces returns values with a continuation function that is invoked with the result. For example, a function in the usual return-value style def f(x: Int): String that takes an integer and returns a string, is in continuation passing style def f(x: Int, k: String => Unit).

Resources. To prepare for this question, revisit
• Slides: Tail Recursion

Question. Consider the following tail-recursive implementation of the factorial function in Scala, using continuation passing:
```scala
def fact(n: Int, k: Int => Unit) = Unit {
  if (n == 0) {
    k(1)
  } else {
    fact(n - 1, resultOfNMinusOne => (k(n * resultOfNMinusOne)))
  }
}
```
Which of the following continuation functions fits the expected signature of k and prints the result to the console:
A: (x: List[Int]) => println(x)
B: x => ()
C: fact(_)
D: (x: Int) => println(x)
E: (x: Int) => x*1

Solution Strategy.
- Match the argument type of function k(Int) with the type left of the => of the continuation function in the answer
- Check the right-hand side of => for performing the requested functionality (println)

Variations.
- Change f (zs, z :: zs) to f (zs, zs)
- f* as a function type t: Int=>String
- f* as a function type t: (Int, String=>Unit) => Unit

**Exercise 7**
JavaScript uses delegation between objects instead of inheritance between classes. To this end, every object has a field `.proto_` pointing to another object that offers functionality for reuse. This field is automatically initialized when using `new` together with a constructor function that offers a prototype object. JavaScript objects and the links between them can be updated dynamically at runtime.

**Resources:**
To prepare for this question, revisit
- Slides: Delegation-based OOP
- Elegant JavaScript: Prototypes

**Question:**
Consider the following JavaScript code:

```javascript
function Box(x) {
    this.x = x;
}
Box.prototype.getX = function() { return this.x; }

let b = new Box(2);
console.log(b.getX());
b.y = 3;

let c = new Box(4);
console.log(c.getX());

c._proto_ = b;
console.log(c.y);

Box.prototype.z = 5;
console.log(c.z);
```

What is printed to the console when this code is executed?
A: 2 undefined undefined
B: An exception is thrown in line 8
C: 2 4 3 5
D: 2 2 3 5
E: An exception is thrown in line 13

**Solution Strategy:**
- Look up names of fields and methods in the current object; if not found, follow the `.proto_` link to search the "parent" object recursively

• Slides Delegation-based OOP
• Eloquent JavaScript Prototypes

Question. Consider the following JavaScript code:

```javascript
function Box(x) {
    this.x = x;
}
Box.prototype.getx = function() { return this.x; }

let b = new Box(2);
console.log(b.getx());
b.y = 3;

let c = new Box(4);
console.log(c.getx());
c.__proto__ = b;
console.log(c.y);
Box.prototype.z = 5;
console.log(c.z);

What is printed to the console when this code is executed?
A: 2 undefined undefined
B: An exception is thrown in line 8
C: 2 4 5
D: 2 2 3 5
E: An exception is thrown in line 13
```

Solution Strategy.
Look up names of fields and methods in the current object; if not found, follow the __proto__ link to search the "parent" object recursively

Variations:
- Change b.y = 3; to b.z = 3;
- Remove b.y = 3;
- Change Box.prototype.z = 5; to Box.prototype.y = 5;
- Remove Box.prototype.z = 5;

This field is automatically initialized when using new together with a constructor function that offers a prototype object. JavaScript objects and the links between them can be updated dynamically at runtime.

Resources.
To prepare for this question, revisit
- Slides Delegation-based OOP
- Eloquent JavaScript: Prototypes

Question.
Consider the following JavaScript code:

```javascript
function Box (x) {
    this.x = x;
}
Box.prototype.getX = function() { return this.x; }

let b = new Box(2);
console.log(b.getX());
b.y = 3;

let c = new Box(4);
console.log(c.getX());

c.__proto__ = b;
console.log(c.y);

Box.prototype.z = 5;
console.log(c.z);
```

What is printed to the console when the code is executed?

============================================================

Consider the following JavaScript code:

```javascript
function Box (x) {
    this.x = x;
}
Box.prototype.getX = function() { return this.x; }

let b = new Box(2);
console.log(b.getX());
b.y = 3;

let c = new Box(4);
console.log(c.getX());

c.__proto__ = b;
console.log(c.y);

Box.prototype.z = 5;
console.log(c.z);
```

What is printed to the console when the code is executed?

============================================================
时间戳: 01:07:20 (4040.00s)
============================================================
Exercise 7
JavaScript uses delegation between objects instead of inheritance between classes. To this end, every object has a field __proto__ pointing to another object that offers functionality for reuse. This field is automatically initialized when using new together with a constructor function that offers a prototype object. JavaScript objects and the links between them can be updated dynamically at runtime.

Resources.

Exercise 7
JavaScript uses delegation between objects instead of inheritance between classes. To this end, every object has a field __proto__ pointing to another object that offers functionality for reuse. This field is automatically initialized when using new together with a constructor function that offers a prototype object. JavaScript objects and the links between them can be updated dynamically at runtime.

JavaScript uses delegation between objects instead of inheritance between classes. To this end, every object has a field __proto__ pointing to another object that offers functionality for reuse. This field is automatically initialized when using new together with a constructor function that offers a prototype object. JavaScript objects and the links between them can be updated dynamically at runtime.

Resources.
To prepare for this question, revisit
- Slides Delegation-based OOP
- Eloquent JavaScript: Prototypes

Question.
Consider the following JavaScript code:

```javascript
function Box (x) {
    this.x = x;
}
Box.prototype.getX = function() { return this.x; }

let b = new Box(2);
console.log(b.getX());
b.y = 3;

let c = new Box(4);
console.log(c.getX());

c.__proto__ = b;
console.log(c.y);

Box.prototype.z = 5;
console.log(c.z);
```

Question.
Consider the following JavaScript code:

```javascript
function Box (x) {
    this.x = x;
}
Box.prototype.getX = function() { return this.x; }

let b = new Box(2);
console.log(b.getX());
b.y = 3;

let c = new Box(4);
console.log(c.getX());

c.__proto__ = b;
console.log(c.y);

Box.prototype.z = 5;
console.log(c.z);
```

What is printed to the console when the code is executed?

============================================================
时间戳: 01:08:42 (4122.00s)
============================================================
Exercise 7
JavaScript uses delegation between objects instead of inheritance between classes. To this end, every object has a field __proto__ pointing to another object that offers functionality for reuse. This field is automatically initialized when using new together with a constructor function that offers a prototype object. JavaScript objects and the links between them can be updated dynamically at runtime.

function Box (x) {
this.x = x;
}
Box.prototype.getX = function() { return this.x; }
let b = new Box(2);
console.log(b.x); // 2
b.y = 3;
let c = new Box(3);
console.log(c.x); // 3
c.__proto__.getX = function() { return this.x + 1; }
Box.prototype.getX = function() { return this.x + 2; }
console.log(b.getX()); // 4
console.log(c.getX()); // 4

Question. Consider the following JavaScript code:

```javascript
function Box(x) {
    this.x = x;
}
Box.prototype.getX = function() { return this.x; }

let b = new Box(2);
console.log(b.getX());
b.y = 3;

let c = new Box(4);
console.log(c.getX());

c.__proto__ = b;
console.log(c.y);

Box.prototype.z = 5;
console.log(c.z);
```

Solution Strategy.

Variations.
• Change b.y = 3; to b.z = 3;
• Remove b.y = 3;
• Change Box.prototype.z = 5; to Box.prototype.y = 5;
• Remove Box.prototype.z = 5;

Question. Consider the following JavaScript code:

```javascript
function Box(x) {

Serial Number: 10

Exercise 8 JavaScript objects are created from object literals enclosed in {}. This syntax choice is somewhat unfortunate since code blocks are also delimited by {}, so carefully inspect whether braces are blocks of statements or enclose a comma-separated list of key: value pairs. Unlike in other languages, accessing fields and methods from within an object requires this. Exercise 8
JavaScript objects are created from object literals enclosed in {}. This syntax choice is somewhat unfortunate since code blocks are also delimited by {}, so carefully inspect whether braces are blocks of statements or enclose a comma-separated list of key: value pairs. Unlike in other languages, accessing fields and methods from within an object requires this. Whenever we attempt to access a field that is not present in an object, JavaScript returns undefined (sometimes throws exceptions) rather than reporting a compile error.

Resources.

        get: function () { return this.n; }
    }
}

function g () {
    var n = 0;
    return {
        get: function () { return n; }
    }
}

var f1 = f ();
var g1 = g ();
```

Exercise 8
JavaScript objects are created from object literals enclosed in {}. This syntax choice is somewhat unfortunate since code blocks are also delimited by {}, so carefully inspect whether braces are blocks of statements or enclose a comma-separated list of key: value pairs. Unlike in other languages, accessing fields and methods from within an object requires this. Whenever we attempt to access a field that is not present in an object, JavaScript returns undefined (sometimes throws exceptions) rather than reporting a compile error.

×
Exercise 8 JavaScript objects are created from object literals enclosed in {}. This syntax choice is somewhat unfortunate since code blocks are also delimited by {}, so carefully inspect whether braces are blocks of statements or enclose a comma-separated list of key: value pairs. Unlike in other languages, accessing fields and methods from within an object requires this. Whenever we attempt to access a field that is not present in an object, JavaScript returns undefined (sometimes throws exceptions) rather than reporting a compile error.

Question. Consider the following JavaScript code:

```javascript
function f () {
    return {
        n: 0,
        get: function () { return this.n; }
    }
}

function g () {
    var n = 0;
    return {
        get: function () { return n; }
    }
}

var f1 = f ();
var g1 = g ();
var g2 = g ();

Identify all of the statements that are true:
1. f1.n returns undefined or throws an exception
2. g1.n returns undefined or throws an exception
3. f1.get() returns undefined or throws an exception
4. g1.get() returns undefined or throws an exception
5. The n used by g1 and g2 is shared between them
A: 1 and 3
B: none are true
```

Exercise 8
JavaScript objects are created from object literals enclosed in {}. This syntax choice is somewhat unfortunate since code blocks are also delimited by {}, so carefully inspect whether braces are blocks of statements or enclose a comma-separated list of key: value pairs. Unlike in other languages, accessing fields and methods from within an object requires this. Whenever we attempt to access a field that is not present in an object, JavaScript returns undefined (sometimes throws exceptions) rather than reporting a compile error.

Resources.
To prepare for this question, revisit
- Slides Delegation-Based OOP
- Eloquent JavaScript: Objects

Question.
Consider the following JavaScript code:

```javascript
function f () {
    return {
        n: 0,
        get: function () { return this.n; }
    }
}

function g () {
    var n = 0;
    return {
        get: function () { return n; }
    }
}
```

Question. Consider the following JavaScript code:

```javascript
function f() {
    return {
        n: 0,
        get: function () { return this.n; }
    }
}

function g() {
    var n = 0;
    return {
        get: function () { return n; }
    }
}

var f1 = f();
var g1 = g();
var g2 = g();
```

Identify all of the statements that are true:
1. f1.n returns undefined or throws an exception
2. g1.n returns undefined or throws an exception
3. f1.get() returns undefined or throws an exception
4. g1.get() returns undefined or throws an exception
5. The n used by g1 and g2 is shared between them

A: 1 and 3
B: none are true
C: 2 and 4
D: 2
E: 1 and 3 and 5

Question. Consider the following JavaScript code:
```javascript
function f () {
  return {
    n: 0,
    get: function () { return this.n; }
  };
}
var g1 = f();
var g2 = g1.get();
```
Identify all of the statements that are true:
1. f1.n returns undefined or throws an exception
2. g1.n returns undefined or throws an exception
3. f1.get() returns undefined or throws an exception
4. g1.get() returns undefined or throws an exception
5. The n used by g1 and g2 is shared between them

A: 1 and 3
B: none are true
C: 2 and 4
D: 2

This appears to be a screenshot of a computer screen showing a terminal window with Node.js running. The terminal is displaying a JavaScript code snippet that demonstrates the use of closures.

The code defines two functions, `f` and `g`, which return objects with a `get` method. The `n` property of these objects is intended to be private, but due to the way the code is written, it is not private as expected.

Here is the code:

```javascript
function f () {
    return {
        n: 0,
        get: function () { return this.n; }
    }
}

function g () {
    var n = 0;
    return {
        get: function () { return n; }
    }
}

var f1 = f ();
var g1 = g ();
var g2 = g ();

console.log(g1.n); // This will output undefined because g1.n is not accessible outside the scope of the returned object.
console.log(g2.n); // This will output 0 because g2.n is accessible within the scope of the returned object.
```

The output of the code is:
```
undefined
0
```

The issue here is that the `n` property in the `g` function is a global variable, so it can be accessed from any scope. To make the `n` property private, you should use an arrow function instead of a regular function for the `get` method, like this:

```javascript
function f () {
    return {
        n: 0,
        get: () => { return this.n; }
    }
}

function g () {
    var n = 0;
    return {
        get: () => { return n; }
    }
}
```

With this change, the `n` property will be private and cannot be accessed from outside the scope of the returned object.
```

时间戳: 01:33:39 (5619.00s)

This appears to be a long document. Save time by reading a summary using AI Assistant.
By using this service, you agree to the Adobe Terms of Use and Privacy Policy.

```
return {
    get: function () { return n; }
}
```

var f1 = f ();
var g1 = g ();
var g2 = g ();

Identify all of the statements that are true:
1. f1.n returns undefined or throws an exception
2. g1.n returns undefined or throws an exception
3. f1.get() returns undefined or throws an exception
4. g1.get() returns undefined or throws an exception
5. The n used by g1 and g2 is shared between them

A: 1 and 3
B: none are true
C: 2 and 4
D: 2
E: 1 and 3 and 5

Solution Strategy.
• Notice that each of the functions returns an object; some declare local variables before returning the object
• When this is present, look for a field in the same object; otherwise look for a local variable. If not present: undefined
• Every time a function is called, new local variables are placed on the stack and added to closures (if accessed from the returned object)

Variations.
• Change return this.n in function f to return n

Identify all of the statements that are true:
1. f1.n returns undefined or throws an exception
2. g1.n returns undefined or throws an exception
3. f1.get() returns undefined or throws an exception
4. g1.get() returns undefined or throws an exception
5. The n used by g1 and g2 is shared between them

A: 1 and 3
B: none are true
C: 2 and 4
D: 2
E: 1 and 3 and 5

Solution Strategy.
- Notice that each of the functions returns an object; some declare local variables before returning the object
- When this is present, look for a field in the same object; otherwise look for a local variable. If not present: undefined
- Every time a function is called, new local variables are placed on the stack and added to closures (if accessed from the returned object)

Variations.
- Change return this.n in function f to return n
- Change return n in function g to return this.n

15 var f1 = f ();
16 var g1 = g ();
17 var g2 = g ();

Identify all of the statements that are true:
1. f1.n returns undefined or throws an exception
2. g1.n returns undefined or throws an exception
3. f1.get() returns undefined or throws an exception
4. g1.get() returns undefined or throws an exception
5. The n used by g1 and g2 is shared between them

A: 1 and 3
B: none are true
C: 2 and 4
D: 2
E: 1 and 3 and 5

Solution Strategy.
- Notice that each of the functions returns an object; some declare local variables before returning the object
- When this is present, look for a field in the same object; otherwise look for a local variable. If not present: undefined
- Every time a function is called, new local variables are placed on the stack and added to closures (if accessed from the returned object)

Variations.
- Change return this.n in function f to return n
- Change return n in function g to return this.n

15 var f1 = f ();
16 var g1 = g ();
17 var g2 = g ();

Identify all of the statements that are true:
1. f1.n returns undefined or throws an exception
2. g1.n returns undefined or throws an exception
3. f1.get() returns undefined or throws an exception
4. g1.get() returns undefined or throws an exception
5. The n used by g1 and g2 is shared between them

A: 1 and 3
B: none are true
C: 2 and 4
D: 2
E: 1 and 3 and 5

Solution Strategy.
- Notice that each of the functions returns an object; some declare local variables before returning the object
- When this is present, look for a field in the same object; otherwise look for a local variable. If not present: undefined
- Every time a function is called, new local variables are placed on the stack and added to closures (if accessed from the returned object)

Variations.
- Change return this.n in function f to return n
- Change return n in function g to return this.n

14 Serial Number: 10

Exercise 14 In object-oriented programming, subclasses can override inherited methods of their base class with a different implementation. As a result, an object of such a subclass has multiple methods of the same name and signature. A programming language's design chooses how to resolve a method call: static dispatch/lookup/binding (early binding) chooses between the methods at compile time based on the static type of the variable holding the object; dynamic dispatch/lookup/binding (late binding) chooses between the methods at runtime based on the dynamic type of the object itself. C++ uses dynamic dispatch/lookup/binding (late binding) only if both of the following conditions are met: the method must be marked virtual and the variable must be a pointer or reference to the object; if at least one of these conditions is violated, C++ uses static dispatch/lookup/binding.

Resources. To prepare for this question, revisit
• Slides: Dynamic Dispatch and Inheritance
• Concepts in Programming Languages: Chapter 12 Objects and Runtime Efficiency: C++

Question. Consider the C++ definitions:
class C { virtual int f() { return 0; } };

What is printed when running this program using a programming language where argument passing is (a) call-by-value; and (b) call-by-reference?
A: Call-by-value:
Call-by-reference:

B: Call-by-value:
Call-by-reference:

C: Call-by-value:
Call-by-reference:

D: Call-by-value:
Call-by-reference:

E: Call-by-value:
Call-by-reference:


Solution Strategy.
- Call-by-value: none of the modifications made inside the called function are visible outside, the variables x and y remain unchanged
- Call-by-reference: update the value of variable x according to the modifications made to a, then update the value of variable y according to the modifications made to b


Variations.
- Change b=b+1 to b=a+1
- Change a=b to a+=1 and also change b=b+1 to b=a+1
- Change f(x, y) to f(x, x)

Serial Number: 10

Exercise 20 In languages with parametric polymorphism, subtyping relationships extend beyond class inheritance relationships. Type covariance, contravariance, and invariance refer to the way how the subtyping relationship between parameterized classes relates to the subtyping relationship of the type parameters. A parameterized type T[.] is covariant if A <: B implies T[A] <: T[B]; for a contravariant type we have A <: B implies T[B] <: T[A]; for an invariant type we have A => B implies T[A] => T[B] (the types are incomparable). Scala lists are covariant. Scala arrays are invariant. Wildcard class parameters allow us to parameterize with an unknown type of a certain bound: T[? <: A] means we parameterize T with an unknown subtype of A (? <: A). As a result, the elements in T are readable as statically typed A. We cannot modify an instance of T because doing so would require us to create instances of ? (an unknown type).

Resources. To prepare for this question, revisit
- Slides Subtyping
- Programming in Scala Chapter 18 Type Parameterization

Exercise 22 JavaScript distinguishes variable declarations in function scope (var) from block scope (let). Variables declared in function scope, are hoisted to the top of the function regardless of their place in the source code, while the initialization remains as an assignment in that place. This can lead to surprising effects together with closures.
Resources. To prepare for this question, revisit
• Slides Surprising Design Decisions
• Eloquent JavaScript: Bindings and Scopes
Question. Consider the following Javascript code with alternative variable declaration keywords:
function () {
    var fs = [];
    for (var i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
        // how does the behavior change with var vs. let?
        var x = i;
        let x = i;
        fs.push (function () { return x; });
    }
    console.log (fs[0] ());
}
Recall that [] is an empty array in JavaScript, and the push method on an array adds a new element to the right-hand side of the array. What is printed to the console when this code is executed?
A. var x=i prints 4 whereas let x=i prints 0

============================================================
Exercise 22
JavaScript distinguishes variable declarations in function scope (var) from block scope (let). Variables declared in function scope, are hoisted to the top of the function regardless of their place in the source code, while the initialization remains as an assignment in that place. This can lead to surprising effects together with closures.

Resources.
To prepare for this question, revisit
- Slides Surprising Design Decisions
- Eloquent JavaScript: Bindings and Scopes

Question.
Consider the following JavaScript code with alternative variable declaration keywords:

```javascript
function () {
    var fs = [];

    for (var i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
        // how does the behavior change with var vs. let?
        var x = i;
        let x = i;
        fs.push(function () { return x; });
    }

    console.log(fs[0]());
}
```

Recall that [] is an empty array in JavaScript, and the push method on an array adds a new element to the right-hand side of the array. What is printed to the console when this code is executed?

A: var x=i prints 4 whereas let x=i prints 0
B: var x=i prints 4 whereas let x=i prints 4
C: var x=i prints 5 whereas let x=i prints 1
D: var x=i prints 0 whereas let x=i prints 0
E: var x=i prints 0 whereas let x=i prints 4

Consider the following JavaScript code with alternative variable declaration keywords:

```javascript
function () {
    var fs = [];

    for (var i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
        // how does the behavior change with var vs. let?
        var x = i;
        let x = i;
        fs.push(function () { return x; });
    }

    console.log(fs[0]());
}
```

Recall that [] is an empty array in JavaScript, and the push method on an array adds a new element to the right-hand side of the array. What is printed to the console when this code is executed?

A: var x=i prints 4 whereas let x=i prints 0
B: var x=i prints 4 whereas let x=i prints 4
C: var x=i prints 5 whereas let x=i prints 1
D: var x=i prints 0 whereas let x=i prints 0
E: var x=i prints 0 whereas let x=i prints 4

时间戳: 02:07:29 (7649.00s)
============================================================
Exercise 22
JavaScript distinguishes variable declarations in function scope (var) from block scope (let). Variables declared in function scope, are hoisted to the top of the function regardless of their place in the source code, while the initialization remains as an assignment in that place. This can lead to surprising effects together with closures.

Exercise 22
JavaScript distinguishes variable declarations in function scope (var) from block scope (let). Variables declared in function scope, are hoisted to the top of the function regardless of their place in the source code, while the initialization remains as an assignment in that place. This can lead to surprising effects together with closures.

Exercise 22
JavaScript distinguishes variable declarations in function scope (var) from block scope (let). Variables declared in function scope, are hoisted to the top of the function regardless of their place in the source code, while the initialization remains as an assignment in that place. This can lead to surprising effects together with closures.

Resources.
To prepare for this question, revisit
- Slides Surprising Design Decisions
- Eloquent JavaScript: Bindings and Scopes

Question.
Consider the following JavaScript code with alternative variable declaration keywords:

```javascript
function () {
    var fs = [];

    for (var i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
        // how does the behavior change with var vs. let?
        var x = i;
        let x = i;
        fs.push(function () { return x; });
    }

    console.log(fs[0]());
}
```

Recall that [] is an empty array in JavaScript, and the push method on an array adds a new element to the right-hand side of the array. What is printed to the console when this code is executed?

A: var x=i prints 4 whereas let x=i prints 0

Exercise 22
JavaScript distinguishes variable declarations in function scope (var) from block scope (let). Variables declared in function scope, are hoisted to the top of the function regardless of their place in the source code, while the initialization remains as an assignment in that place. This can lead to surprising effects together with closures.

JavaScript distinguishes variable declarations in function scope (var) from block scope (let). Variables declared in function scope, are hoisted to the top of the function regardless of their place in the source code, while the initialization remains as an assignment in that place. This can lead to surprising effects together with closures.

Exercise 22
JavaScript distinguishes variable declarations in function scope (var) from block scope (let). Variables declared in function scope, are hoisted to the top of the function regardless of their place in the source code, while the initialization remains as an assignment in that place. This can lead to surprising effects together with closures.

Resources.
To prepare for this question, revisit
- Slides Surprising Design Decisions
- Eloquent JavaScript: Bindings and Scopes

Question.
Consider the following JavaScript code with alternative variable declaration keywords:

```javascript
function () {
    var fs = [];

    for (var i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
        // how does the behavior change with var vs. let?
        var x = i;
        let x = i;
        fs.push(function () { return x; });
    }

    console.log(fs[0]());
}
```

This can lead to surprising effects together with closures.

Resources.
To prepare for this question, revisit
- Slides Surprising Design Decisions
- Eloquent JavaScript: Bindings and Scopes

Question.
Consider the following JavaScript code with alternative variable declaration keywords:

```javascript
function () {
    var fs = [];

    for (var i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
        // how does the behavior change with var vs. let?
        var x = i;
        let x = i;
        fs.push(function () { return x; });
    }

    console.log(fs[0]());
}
```

Recall that [] is an empty array in JavaScript, and the push method on an array adds a new element to the right-hand side of the array. What is printed to the console when this code is executed?

A: var x=i prints 4 whereas let x=i prints 0
B: var x=i prints 4 whereas let x=i prints 4
C: var x=i prints 5 whereas let x=i prints 1
D: var x=i prints 0 whereas let x=i prints 0
E: var x=i prints 0 whereas let x=i prints 4

    for (var i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
        // how does the behavior change with var vs. let?
        var x = i;
        let x = i;
        fs.push(function () { return x; });
    }

    console.log(fs[0]());
}
```

Recall that [] is an empty array in JavaScript, and the push method on an array adds a new element to the right-hand side of the array. What is printed to the console when this code is executed?

A: var x=i prints 4 whereas let x=i prints 0
B: var x=i prints 4 whereas let x=i prints 4
C: var x=i prints 5 whereas let x=i prints 1
D: var x=i prints 0 whereas let x=i prints 0
E: var x=i prints 0 whereas let x=i prints 4

Exercise 22
JavaScript distinguishes variable declarations in function scope (var) from block scope (let). Variables declared in function scope, are hoisted to the top of the function regardless of their place in the source code, while the initialization remains as an assignment in that place. This can lead to surprising effects together with closures.

Exercise 22
JavaScript distinguishes variable declarations in function scope (var) from block scope (let). Variables declared in function scope, are hoisted to the top of the function regardless of their place in the source code, while the initialization remains as an assignment in that place. This can lead to surprising effects together with closures.

Exercise 22
JavaScript distinguishes variable declarations in function scope (var) from block scope (let). Variables declared in function scope, are hoisted to the top of the function regardless of their place in the source code, while the initialization remains as an assignment in that place. This can lead to surprising effects together with closures.

Resources.
To prepare for this question, revisit
- Slides Surprising Design Decisions
- Eloquent JavaScript: Bindings and Scopes

Question.
Consider the following JavaScript code with alternative variable declaration keywords:

```javascript
function () {
    var fs = [];

    for (var i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
        // how does the behavior change with var vs. let?
        var x = i;
        let x = i;
        fs.push(function () { return x; });
    }

    console.log(fs[0]());
}
```

Recall that [] is an empty array in JavaScript, and the push method on an array adds a new element to the right-hand side of the array. What is printed to the console when this code is executed?

Exercise 22
JavaScript distinguishes variable declarations in function scope (var) from block scope (let). Variables declared in function scope, are hoisted to the top of the function regardless of their place in the source code, while the initialization remains as an assignment in that place. This can lead to surprising effects together with closures.

Exercise 22
JavaScript distinguishes variable declarations in function scope (var) from block scope (let). Variables declared in function scope, are hoisted to the top of the function regardless of their place in the source code, while the initialization remains as an assignment in that place. This can lead to surprising effects together with closures.

- Leave let x = i in place, then evaluate the code

 <ul><li>For var x = i, move var x to the top of the function, leave x = i in place, then evaluate the code</li><li>Leave let x = i in place, then evaluate the code</li></ul> 
 <h2>Variations.</h2> 
 <ul><li>Remove var x=i and directly access i from the functions added to the array</li><li>Change for (var i=0; ... ) to for (let i=0; ...) and directly access i from the functions added to the array</li></ul> 
</body></html>
```

时间戳: 02:11:44 (7904.00s)

// how does the behavior change with var vs. let?
var x = i;
let x = i;
fs.push(function () { return x; });

console.log(fs[0] ());

Recall that [] is an empty array in JavaScript, and the push method on an array adds a new element to the right-hand side of the array. What is printed to the console when this code is executed?

A: var x=i prints 4 whereas let x=i prints 0
B: var x=i prints 4 whereas let x=i prints 4
C: var x=i prints 5 whereas let x=i prints 1
D: var x=i prints 0 whereas let x=i prints 0
E: var x=i prints 0 whereas let x=i prints 4

Solution Strategy.
• For var x = i, move var x to the top of the function, leave x = i in place, then evaluate the code
• Leave let x = i in place, then evaluate the code

Variations.
• Remove var x=i and directly access i from the functions added to the array
• Change for (var i=0; ...) to for (let i=0; ...) and directly access i from the functions added to the array

B: var x=i prints 4 whereas let x=i prints 4
C: var x=i prints 5 whereas let x=i prints 1
D: var x=i prints 0 whereas let x=i prints 0
E: var x=i prints 0 whereas let x=i prints 4

Solution Strategy.
• For var x = i, move var x to the top of the function, leave x = i in place, then evaluate the code
• Leave let x = i in place, then evaluate the code

Variations.
• Remove var x=i and directly access i from the functions added to the array
• Change for (var i=0; ...) to for (let i=0; ...) and directly access i from the functions added to the array

<html><body>
<p>This appears to be a long document. Save time by reading a summary using AI Assistant.</p> 
 <p>By using this service, you agree to the Adobe Terms of Use and Privacy Policy</p> 
 <h2>Question.</h2> 
 <p>Consider the following JavaScript code with alternative variable declaration keywords:</p> 
 <div class="image"><img/></div> 
 <p>Recall that [] is an empty array in JavaScript, and the push method on an array adds a new element to the right-hand side of the array. What is printed to the console when this code is executed?</p> 
 <p>A: var x=i prints 4 whereas let x=i prints 0</p> 
 <p>B: var x=i prints 4 whereas let x=i prints 4</p> 
 <p>C: var x=i prints 5 whereas let x=i prints 1</p> 
 <p>D: var x=i prints 0 whereas let x=i prints 0</p> 
 <p>E: var x=i prints 0 whereas let x=i prints 4</p> 
 <h2>Solution Strategy.</h2> 
 <ul><li>For var x = i, move var x to the top of the function, leave x = i in place, then evaluate the code</li><li>Leave let x = i in place, then evaluate the code</li></ul> 
 <h2>Variations.</h2> 
 <ul><li>Remove var x=i and directly access i from the functions added to the array</li><li>Change for (var i=0; ... ) to for (let i=0; ...) and directly access i from the functions added to the array</li></ul> 
</body></html>

Question. Consider the following JavaScript code with alternative variable declaration keywords:
```javascript
function () {
    var fs = [];

    for (var i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
        // how does the behavior change with var vs. let?
        var x = i;
        let x = i;
        fs.push(function () { return x; });
    }

    console.log(fs[0] ());
}
```

Recall that [] is an empty array in JavaScript, and the push method on an array adds a new element to the right-hand side of the array. What is printed to the console when this code is executed?
A: var x=i prints 4 whereas let x=i prints 0
B: var x=i prints 4 whereas let x=i prints 4
C: var x=i prints 5 whereas let x=i prints 1
D: var x=i prints 0 whereas let x=i prints 0
E: var x=i prints 0 whereas let x=i prints 4

Solution Strategy.
- For var x = i, move var x to the top of the function, leave x = i in place, then evaluate the code
- Leave let x = i in place, then evaluate the code

Variations.
- Remove var x=i and directly access i from the functions added to the array
- Change for (var i=0; ...) to for (let i=0; ...) and directly access i from the functions added to the array

```markdown
Question. Consider the following JavaScript code with alternative variable declaration keywords:

```javascript
function () {
    var fs = [];

    for (var i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
        // how does the behavior change with var vs. let?
        var x = i;
        let x = i;
        fs.push(function () { return x; });
    }

    console.log(fs[0] ());
}
```

Recall that [] is an empty array in JavaScript, and the push method on an array adds a new element to the right-hand side of the array. What is printed to the console when this code is executed?

A: var x=i prints 4 whereas let x=i prints 0
B: var x=i prints 4 whereas let x=i prints 4
C: var x=i prints 5 whereas let x=i prints 1
D: var x=i prints 0 whereas let x=i prints 0
E: var x=i prints 0 whereas let x=i prints 4

Solution Strategy.
- For var x = i, move var x to the top of the function, leave x = i in place, then evaluate the code
- Leave let x = i in place, then evaluate the code

Variations.
- Remove var x=i and directly access i from the functions added to the array
- Change for (var i=0; ...) to for (let i=0; ...) and directly access i from the functions added to the array
```

Question. Consider the following JavaScript code with alternative variable declaration keywords:

```javascript
function() {
    var fs = [];

    for (var i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
        // how does the behavior change with var vs. let?
        var x = i;
        let x = i;

        fs.push(function() { return x; });
    }

    console.log(fs[0]());
}
```

Recall that [] is an empty array in JavaScript, and the push method on an array adds a new element to the right-hand side of the array. What is printed to the console when this code is executed?

A: var x=i prints 4 whereas let x=i prints 0
B: var x=i prints 4 whereas let x=i prints 4
C: var x=i prints 5 whereas let x=i prints 1
D: var x=i prints 0 whereas let x=i prints 0
E: var x=i prints 0 whereas let x=i prints 4

Solution Strategy.
- For var x = i, move var x to the top of the function, leave x = i in place, then evaluate the code
- Leave let x = i in place, then evaluate the code

Variations.
- Remove var x=i and directly access i from the functions added to the array
- Change for (var i=0; ...) to for (let i=0; ...) and directly access i from the functions added to the array

**Question.** Consider the following JavaScript code with alternative variable declaration keywords:

```javascript
function() {
    var fs = [];

    for (var i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
        // how does the behavior change with var vs. let?
        var x = i;
        let x = i;
        fs.push(function() { return x; });
    }

    console.log(fs[0]());
}
```

Recall that [] is an empty array in JavaScript, and the push method on an array adds a new element to the right-hand side of the array. What is printed to the console when this code is executed?

A: var x=i prints 4 whereas let x=i prints 0
B: var x=i prints 4 whereas let x=i prints 4
C: var x=i prints 5 whereas let x=i prints 1
D: var x=i prints 0 whereas let x=i prints 0
E: var x=i prints 0 whereas let x=i prints 4

**Solution Strategy.**
- For var x = i, move var x to the top of the function, leave x = i in place, then evaluate the code
- Leave let x = i in place, then evaluate the code

**Variations.**
- Remove var x=i and directly access i from the functions added to the array
- Change for (var i=0; ...) to for (let i=0; ...) and directly access i from the functions added to the array

Question. Consider the following JavaScript code with alternative variable declaration keywords:
```javascript
function () {
    var fs = [];

    for (var i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
        // how does the behavior change with var vs. let?
        var x = i;
        let x = i;
        fs.push(function () { return x; });
    }

    console.log(fs[0] ());
}
```
Recall that [] is an empty array in JavaScript, and the push method on an array adds a new element to the right-hand side of the array. What is printed to the console when this code is executed?
A: var x=i prints 4 whereas let x=i prints 0
B: var x=i prints 4 whereas let x=i prints 4
C: var x=i prints 5 whereas let x=i prints 1
D: var x=i prints 0 whereas let x=i prints 0
E: var x=i prints 0 whereas let x=i prints 4

Solution Strategy.
- For var x = i, move var x to the top of the function, leave x = i in place, then evaluate the code
- Leave let x = i in place, then evaluate the code

Variations.
- Remove var x=i and directly access i from the functions added to the array
- Change for (var i=0; ...) to for (let i=0; ...) and directly access i from the functions added to the array

This appears to be a long document. Save time by reading a summary using AI Assistant.
By using this service, you agree to the Adobe Terms of Use and Privacy Policy.

Question. Consider the following JavaScript code with alternative variable declaration keywords:
```javascript
function () {
    var fs = [];

    for (var i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
        // how does the behavior change with var vs. let?
        var x = i;
        let x = i;
        fs.push(function () { return x; });
    }

    console.log(fs[0] ());
}
```

Recall that [] is an empty array in JavaScript, and the push method on an array adds a new element to the right-hand side of the array. What is printed to the console when this code is executed?
A: var x=i prints 4 whereas let x=i prints 0
B: var x=i prints 4 whereas let x=i prints 4
C: var x=i prints 1 whereas let x=i prints 0
D: var x=i prints 0 whereas let x=i prints 0
E: var x=i prints 0 whereas let x=i prints 4

Solution S
- For the first function, leave x = i in place, then evaluate the code
- Leave the second function as is

Question. Consider the following JavaScript code with alternative variable declaration keywords:

```javascript
function () {
    var fs = [];

    for (var i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
        // how does the behavior change with var vs. let?
        var x = i;
        let x = i;
        fs.push(function () { return x; });
    }

    console.log(fs[0]());
}
```

Recall that [] is an empty array in JavaScript, and the push method on an array adds a new element to the right-hand side of the array. What is printed to the console when this code is executed?

A: var x=i prints 4 whereas let x=i prints 0
B: var x=i prints 4 whereas let x=i prints 4
C: var x=i prints 5 whereas let x=i prints 1
D: var x=i prints 0 whereas let x=i prints 0
E: var x=i prints 0 whereas let x=i prints 4

Solution Strategy.
- For var x = i, move var x to the top of the function, leave x = i in place, then evaluate the code
- Leave let x = i in place, then evaluate the code

Variations.
- Remove var x=i and directly access i from the functions added to the array
- Change for (var i=0; ...) to for (let i=0; ...) and directly access i from the functions added to the array
```

Question. Consider the following JavaScript code with alternative variable declaration keywords:

```javascript
function () {
    var fs = [];

    for (var i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
        // how does the behavior change with var vs. let?

        let x = i;
        fs.push(function () { return x; });
    }

    console.log(fs[0]());
}
```

Recall that [] is an empty array in JavaScript, and the push method on an array adds a new element to the right-hand side of the array. What is printed to the console when this code is executed?

A: var x=i prints 4 whereas let x=i prints 0
B: var x=i prints 4 whereas let x=i prints 4
C: var x=i prints 5 whereas let x=i prints 1
D: var x=i prints 0 whereas let x=i prints 0
E: var x=i prints 0 whereas let x=i prints 4

Solution Strategy.
- For var x = i, move var x to the top of the function, leave x = i in place, then evaluate the code
- Leave let x = i in place, then evaluate the code

Variations.
- Remove var x=i and directly access i from the functions added to the array
- Change for (var i=0; ...) to for (let i=0; ...) and directly access i from the functions added to the array
